title: The Ferryman

teacherSummary.text: Siddhartha becomes Vasudeva's assistant. Vasudeva, a simple and attentive listener, teaches him to listen to the river, which shows that there is no such thing as time—the river is everywhere at once. Years pass peacefully. Gotama's monks pass by, carrying news that the Buddha is dying, and Kamala travels with her son to see him; she is bitten by a snake, recognizes Siddhartha at the ferry, and dies in his arms. Siddhartha keeps their son.

Behold, once before you have ferried me across this water in your boat for the immaterial reward of a good deed.
The rich and elegant Siddhartha is becoming an oarsman’s servant, the learned Brahmin Siddhartha becomes a ferryman: this has also been told to you by the river.
He looked up and first saw the boy’s face, which wondrously reminded him of something, like a warning to remember something he had forgotten.

segments.script: The image of the river echoes ancient ideas, such as Heraclitus's saying that one cannot step into the same river twice. The listening river replaces human teachers; Kamala's peaceful death and the son's arrival begin a new test. Characterization: Siddhartha joins Vasudeva the ferryman, who is a perfect listener and says the river taught him everything. Imagery: The river's surface, bubbles, colours, and above all its voices. Plot: Years later Kamala, now a Buddhist follower, comes with her son to see the dying Buddha; she is bitten by a snake and dies in Siddhartha's arms; the boy is Siddhartha's son. Watch for the river: The river teaches unity, simultaneity and listening; it returns in every stage of Siddhartha's life. In this chapter: “By this river I want to stay, thought Siddhartha, it is the same which” (The Ferryman, paragraph 1).

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Love this water! Stay near it! Learn from it” slowly and put it in my own words: Gazing into the river, Siddhartha hears a voice inside him urging him to love the water, stay near it and learn from it. Next, craft. I notice three short commands, each with an exclamation mark, like a calling. The strongest word is “Learn”: it turns the river from scenery into a teacher. Then, effect. What does the river seem to tell Siddhartha? My answer: The river seems to tell Siddhartha to stay and learn from it, so he decides to remain with the ferryman; the line shows that his next teacher will be the river and listening, not a doctrine.
